title: Redwood discovery with Starlight AI

Follow-up: send pricing model and schedule technical deep dive for benchmarks in their VPC testbed.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Cho (Starlight VP ML), Maya Torres (Starlight CTO), Simon Lee (Starlight Sr DE)

[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we'll do discovery and mainly focus on cost per unit economics and deployment options — hosted, dedicated, private — and what levers you can pull.
[00:18] Daniel Cho: Yep thanks Alex. We're on a pretty tight budget this quarter; want to understand where costs come from. We run a mix of chat assistants and batch embeddings for search.
[00:30] Maya Torres: And security is a showstopper for some customers – we need SOC2, customer data residency, and KMS integration.
[00:40] Alex Morgan: Totally. Priya will cover some of the technical knobs later. Just high-level, Redwood hosted gives fastest time-to-value and simpler per-token billing; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput; Private is for VPC or on-prem with more control and usually diferent pricing structure. (sic)
[01:05] Priya Patel: Hi all. Wanted to ask about your workload mix. Daniel you mentioned chat + embeddings, can you give rough qps and tokens per request?
[01:20] Daniel Cho: Sure. Peak qps is around 120 requests per second for chat, avg token output ~220, input tokens ~80. Embeddings are batched overnight — about 200k docs/week, usually 512-dim. Our monthly token consumption is around 1.8B tokens presently.
[01:40] Simon Lee: Important: most chat sessions are short — 1-3 turns — but we do have long context for a small percent. Latency SLOs are 300ms p95 for chat.
[01:55] Alex Morgan: OK cool. On cost levers: per-token pricing matters, but batching, prefix/KV caching, and quantization shift effective cost/unit a lot. For example, batching embeddings can drop per-item CPU/GPU overhead, and KV/prefix caching can avoid repeated prompt tokens so your marginal token cost drops.
[02:20] Maya Torres: How predictable is Dedicated pricing? We dislike surprise bills.
[02:28] Priya Patel: Dedicated is typically reserved capacity with monthly/annual commit. You get guaranteed throughput, which helps amortize host costs. We can model price per token across your 1.8B tokens with different batch sizes and cache hit rates.
[02:45] Daniel Cho: Can you give a concrete example — like hosted per-token vs dedicated per-token?
[02:52] Alex Morgan: High level — hosted lists per-token; with your volume, we can show two buckets: fully hosted at list rate; dedicated we amortize the reserved GPU cost + infra over throughput, so your per-token drop can be significant if you can stay within commit. Private tends to be license+support + infra ops. We'll send spreadsheet.
[03:15] [Priya shares screen?] Priya Patel: I'm going to sketch the levers. First: batching. For embeddings, batch size affects memory and throughput — bigger batches give better GPU utilization and lower per-embedding cost but at potential latency cost. For chat, continuous batching and KV cache reduce repeated input tokens.
[03:40] Simon Lee: How reliable is prefix/KV caching across sessions? Our engineers are worried about cache staleness and consistency across scaled replicas.
[03:49] Priya Patel: Good question. Redwood's runtime manages KV cache per session with consistency guarantees for active sessions; across replicas we sync or do sticky routing depending on policy. In Dedicated we can pin sessions to nodes to avoid cross-node misses. There may be minor imperfect transcription there — sorry, I mean, minor cache miss windows during failover.
[04:15] Maya Torres: Any quantization tradeoffs? We want to keep quality high — some hallucinations are unacceptable for us.
[04:22] Priya Patel: We recommend quantization profiles per-model. 4-bit quant can reduce memory footprint and cost but might affect output distribution slightly. For highest quality, keep FP16 or 8-bit unless you've validated on eval sets. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles per workload.
[04:40] Daniel Cho: Ok, so we need a model that maps our budget to expected latency and quality. Our finance wants an expected monthly spend cap of $25k for inference to start.
[04:52] Alex Morgan: That helps. With 1.8B tokens, rough back-of-envelope — depends on model choice and quoting — but with batching and caching we can usually optimize to meet targets. We'll run scenarios: hosted at list, dedicated with 50% commit, and private TCO with ops costs.
[05:10] [08:30 omitted long pause while they look at doc — transcription imperfect]
[08:45] Simon Lee: Our priority is predictable unit economics. If we go hosted and spike, how do we avoid bill shock?
[08:53] Alex Morgan: We offer quotas, rate limits, and alerts. For customers with tighter budgets, we often recommend dedicated or a hybrid routing policy where low-risk traffic hits hosted, and high-volume pipelines run on Dedicated.
[09:12] Maya Torres: Hybrid sounds interesting. Can Redwood route by policy?
[09:16] Priya Patel: Yes — smart routing by latency, cost, region, or customer tier. You can set automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants when capacity constrained.
[09:28] Daniel Cho: What about VPC/private for regulated customers? We have a few clients requiring air-gapped or strict residency.
[09:35] Alex Morgan: Private deployment supports VPC and on-prem. There's an additional setup and platform fee. You also manage keys via KMS/HSM and we can integrate SSO/SAML and RBAC.
[09:50] Maya Torres: Do you have SOC2 + ISO certs?
[09:53] Alex Morgan: Yes we have SOC2 Type II; we'll share the report and security pack.
[10:02] Daniel Cho: Back to cost: can we simulate different cache hit rates? For example if 30% of tokens are cached because of repeated prefixes, how much does that shift cost?
[10:12] Priya Patel: We can definitely model that. Caching reduces the need to re-send long context; effective tokens billed drop. We'll show a 3-scenario model: no cache, 30% cache hit, 60% cache hit.
[10:28] Simon Lee: For embeddings batching, can we do asynchronous batch windows overnight? That helps with cost but also increases end-to-end latency which is OK for search recency.
[10:36] Alex Morgan: Yes, batch windows are a typical cost optimization for embeddings. Redwood supports scheduled batch jobs and we can recommend batch sizes vs VM/GPU types.
[10:48] Daniel Cho: Are there fixed costs hidden in dedicated? Like support tiers, reserved infra, etc?
[10:53] Alex Morgan: There is reserved capacity commit and an ops/support add-on for Private. Dedicated includes the reserved GPU pool; support and advanced observability can be add-ons which we'll show.
[11:05] Maya Torres: For dedicated, how fast can we scale up if demand spikes? We have seasonal load.
[11:11] Priya Patel: Dedicated supports burst capacity options. You can configure autoscale policies and burst to hosted or additional capacity, depending on plan.
[11:22] [12:00 quick crosstalk — someone muted/unmuted]
[12:10] Daniel Cho: One of our engineers asked about accuracy regressions when changing quantization or switching model variants. How does Redwood help guard against that?
[12:18] Priya Patel: We have evals and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts against your test prompts and trigger rollbacks or canarying.
[12:32] Simon Lee: Will you allow us to pin model versions during rollout? We need deterministic behavior for audits.
[12:37] Alex Morgan: Yes — pinning versions and rollouts (canary/A-B) are supported; automatic fallback policies are also available.
[12:45] Maya Torres: Good. On networking: for private, do you require a VPN or peering?
[12:52] Priya Patel: We typically do VPC peering or private link depending on cloud. For on-prem there are connectors. We'll share network diagrams.
[13:05] Daniel Cho: Let's put numbers on the table next. If we assume model X at hosted list rate is $0.00008 per token output (example), what does that look like for us?
[13:18] Alex Morgan: Roughly multiply by your monthly tokens; but again that's only illustrative. We'll send a spreadsheet with per-token examples across model families, plus a Dedicated amortization sheet.
[13:30] Maya Torres: We care about p95 latency at 300ms. If dedicated helps us get that deterministically, that's worth a premium.
[13:37] Priya Patel: Right — Dedicated gives predictable p95; hosted can get there but with multi-tenant variability. We can show benchmarks from similar customers.
[13:50] Daniel Cho: About data retention — how long do you keep logs and do you allow disabling retention?
[13:57] Alex Morgan: We retain logs per account settings. For enterprise we offer configurable retention and can disable retention or send logs to customer-managed storage. We'll include that in security docs.
[14:10] Simon Lee: For the benchmark deep dive, we want to run our Hydra dataset (approx 5k conversations) and measure p95 and per-token cost. Can Redwood run that in our VPC?
[14:20] Priya Patel: Yes, we can plan a VPC-based benchmark or run a dedicated staging environment. We'll need your dataset format and expected concurrency.
[14:32] Daniel Cho: Timeline — if we like the numbers, we'd aim to pilot in Q4 and decide on commit in Q1.
[14:38] Alex Morgan: That's reasonable. We'll get the cost scenarios over to you by Monday and propose slot for the tech deep dive.
[14:45] Maya Torres: Great. A couple of quick questions from Simon: what's the expected delta in per-token cost if we move from FP16 to 4-bit?
[14:55] Priya Patel: Depends on model and hardware; sometimes 20-40% lower memory and cost for inference but you need to validate quality on your eval set. We'll include examples.
[15:05] Simon Lee: One last ask — include the break-even commit level for Dedicated given our profile. Finance wants to know at what commit we beat hosted cost.
[15:13] Alex Morgan: We'll compute break-even commit levels in the sheet.
[15:18] [Wrap-up]
[15:20] Alex Morgan: Quick recap — we'll send: cost model spreadsheet (hosted/dedicated/private), security pack (SOC2/KMS/network), and propose benchmark plan. Priya will draft benchmark steps. Any other asks?
[15:32] Maya Torres: Please include variant/quantization quality caveats and example regressions.
[15:36] Daniel Cho: And the break-even commit number.
[15:39] Simon Lee: We'll share the token distribution and Hydra dataset sample.
[15:42] Alex Morgan: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email.
[15:47] Meeting end.
